answer: In 1937 the Zionist Congress rejected the Peel borders but authorised talks; in 1947 the Jewish community accepted partition; the Arab leadership rejected both. At Khartoum in 1967 Arab states said no peace, no recognition, no negotiations; in 2002 the Arab League offered normal relations for full withdrawal, and Israel replied with reservations. Oslo set up self-government and did not promise a state. In January 2001 Clinton said Barak and Arafat accepted his parameters with reservations; Ross says Arafat did not say yes; Malley and Agha say Barak accepted nothing at Camp David. In 2008 Olmert showed Abbas a map; Abbas has said he rejected it because he was not allowed to study it. In 2020 Netanyahu agreed to negotiate on Trump's plan; Abbas rejected it, citing Jerusalem. Our reading: refusals came from both sides, at different moments.

could_not_verify: Taba: we read the Moratinos non-paper as hosted by the UN and Eldar's Haaretz article, but not the full list of what each side offered on Jerusalem and refugees; Barak's and the Palestinian negotiators' own accounts were not read.
The Road Map: only Israel's refugee reservation is quoted from the cabinet text; we did not read all 14 reservations one by one, or a Palestinian document stating their acceptance (we rely on JTA).

The Kerry talks: Kerry's own account and Netanyahu's and Abbas's own statements on why the talks ended were not read; the blame is given through Indyk, unnamed US officials and Miller, as reported by Reuters (NBC), MERIP and JTA.

Fewer than three reliable sources: Khartoum (Avalon and The Guardian only), the 1947 acceptance and rejection (UN and the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, plus two government pages), the Peel recommendation has three but the Taba and Road Map facts each include an advocacy or government page beyond three reliable ones; the Olmert fact leans on a CFR blog post by a partisan author for Abbas's 2015 words.
Abbas's 2009 statement to the Washington Post that 'the gaps were wide' (the page would not load for us).

Barak's Camp David percentages from a primary document: Malley and Agha say no written offer exists. The Peel report and Dennis Ross's book were not read directly. Podeh's article on Israel's non-response to the Arab Peace Initiative and the Chatham House pages could not be read.
Britannica could not be read by our fetcher, so its pages are not cited.

The Arab leadership's own stated reasons for rejecting partition in 1937 and 1947 (Arab Higher Committee statements) were not read; the card has only the State Department's summary that they thought the plan favourable to the Jews. Netanyahu's own statements on a Palestinian state (Bar-Ilan 2009, 2015, 2024) are not on this card.
not_claimed: Listing who refused what does not by itself assign blame: a refusal can be reasonable, forced by politics, or a mistake, and the card does not rank the refusals.
It does not claim any of these plans would have produced peace, or that Barak's and Olmert's offers were signed texts.
It does not claim Zionist acceptance in 1937 or 1947 was unconditional or sincere, or that Arab refusals were unjustified.
It does not claim Abbas or Arafat spoke for every Palestinian, or that Israel's governments always spoke for every Israeli.
It does not say that the Arab Peace Initiative was an offer Israel should have accepted as written.

answer_claims.says: In 1937 the Zionist Congress rejected the Peel borders but authorised talks; in 1947 the Jewish community accepted partition; the Arab leadership rejected both.
At Khartoum in 1967 Arab states said no peace, no recognition, no negotiations; in 2002 the Arab League offered normal relations for full withdrawal, and Israel replied with reservations.
Oslo set up self-government and did not promise a state.
In January 2001 Clinton said Barak and Arafat accepted his parameters with reservations; Ross says Arafat did not say yes; Malley and Agha say Barak accepted nothing at Camp David.
In 2008 Olmert showed Abbas a map; Abbas has said he rejected it because he was not allowed to study it.
In 2020 Netanyahu agreed to negotiate on Trump's plan; Abbas rejected it, citing Jerusalem.
Our reading: refusals came from both sides, at different moments.

skeptic.notes: Read at least two sources per fact in context; all 70 quotes are on their pages. Strongest Palestinian objection: the card says Arafat 'did not say yes' (Ross) and Abbas 'rejected' Olmert's map, but gave neither man's stated reason; Ross's own NPR answer adds that the Palestinian delegation had decided to accept and Arafat said no. Reasons are now in contested, but the Arab leadership's own words for rejecting 1937 and 1947 are absent (must-fix: needs a new source). Strongest Israeli objection: the card has no Israeli leader's own statement on a Palestinian state (Bar-Ilan 2009, Netanyahu 2015 and 2024), the best evidence for the 'Israel never wanted one' side, and the Arab Peace Initiative claim 'never formally accepted' rests on an advocacy page (Arab Center) plus CFR's 'skepticism'. Fixed by me: Clinton's remarks are dated 7 January 2001, not December 2000; F10 said 'disconnected areas' and 'demilitarised', which no cited page says (BBC quotes Trump promising contiguous territory); F6's State Dept quote was about Camp David, replaced with the Oslo deferral sentence; F2's 56 percent is Khalidi's figure for the UN committee's report; MERIP 'Indyk vs. Indyk' is unsigned, relabelled other; the Abrams blog relabelled advocacy. Not independent or short: F3 has two reliable sources (UN, JTA; State Dept and FRUS are government); F4 has two (Avalon, Guardian); F9 now has two (BBC, AP); F11 and F12 each lean on an advocacy or government page for the Israeli position; F13's 'primary sabotage' claim reaches us only through the unsigned MERIP page, not Barnea's report. Wire: Fox/AP and NBC/Reuters already marked. Should-fix: JTA archive pieces carry no byline we could check; Khalidi is read through an archive.org full-text copy of a book. MUST-FIX list: (1) Arab leadership's stated reasons 1937/1947 in their own words; (2) an Israeli primary statement on a Palestinian state; (3) a third reliable source for F3, F4, F9, F13; (4) a non-advocacy source for 'never formally accepted'.

citer.notes: Split the answer into seven sentences, each tied to facts. Removed: 'Both slogans are too simple' (a verdict no fact carries; the closing 'Our reading' sentence stays); 'the Zionist leadership accepted the principle of partition in 1937' (the UN history on the card says the Congress judged it too early; reworded to what F1 carries: rejected the borders, authorised talks); 'Israel did not accept that as a basis for talks' (single advocacy source; reworded to 'replied with reservations', which CBS carries); 'Barak's were within them and Arafat's were not' (Ross says only that Arafat did not say yes); 'proposals were never fixed offers' (Malley and Agha's quote is about Camp David, not the December parameters; reworded). Added Abbas's stated reasons for 2008 and 2020, which F9 and F10 now carry. Answer is 140 words. Verdict holds for the answer as now worded; the card stays draft because the skeptic verdict is weakened.
